title: Diffusion Language Models After the 2026 Scaling Laws

body:
For three years the discourse around diffusion language models has oscillated between "the successor to autoregressive generation" and "an elegant paper trick that does not scale." The empirical evidence was thin on both sides. A single model trained at one compute budget cannot settle whether a family scales, and nothing short of a scaling law can. In February 2026, Sahoo and colleagues posted the first proper scaling study, training masked, uniform-state, and interpolating discrete diffusion models at matched compute from roughly 100M to 1.7B parameters alongside autoregressive baselines. The headline numbers are not what either side wanted. Masked diffusion needs roughly $14\times$ more FLOPs than an autoregressive model to reach the same validation loss; uniform-state diffusion needs about $23\times$; interpolating variants pay $32\times$. And yet uniform-state diffusion, with the *worst* validation perplexity of the three, posts the best GSM8K accuracy at 1.7B, better than the autoregressive baseline.

## Why this matters now

Two reasons. First, allocating training FLOPs is the single most consequential decision a frontier lab makes, and until this year the diffusion branch could not say whether its 2024–2025 wins were artefacts of particular model sizes. Now we have power-law fits with uncertainties over more than a decade of compute. Second, the GSM8K anomaly is not noise. A string of papers posted through the autumn has shown that diffusion LMs behave differently on multi-step reasoning than their perplexities predict, and the gap widens with inference-time tricks that are unnatural for autoregressive models. Something is going on that validation perplexity cannot see. If your work touches reasoning, evaluation methodology, or the inductive biases of language modelling, you can no longer treat diffusion LMs as "just another decoder."

## The forward process, the ELBO, and the three families

Fix a vocabulary $V$ of size $|V|$. A discrete diffusion language model corrupts a clean sequence $\mathbf{x}_0 \in V^L$ into a sequence of latents $\mathbf{x}_t$ for $t \in [0,1]$ via a time-indexed transition kernel $q(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \mathbf{x}_0)$ that factorises over positions. Three forward processes dominate the literature.

**Masked (absorbing-state).** Introduce a special mask token $\mathtt{M}$. Each clean token independently stays itself or becomes $\mathtt{M}$:

$$q(x_t^i = \mathtt{M} \mid x_0^i) = \alpha_t, \qquad q(x_t^i = x_0^i \mid x_0^i) = 1 - \alpha_t,$$

with a monotone schedule $\alpha_0 = 0$, $\alpha_1 = 1$. Sahoo et al. (2024) showed that under a "SUBS" parameterisation — the denoising network assigns zero probability to $\mathtt{M}$, and already-unmasked tokens are carried through the reverse chain unchanged — the continuous-time ELBO collapses, Rao–Blackwell style, to a time-reweighted masked-token cross-entropy:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{MDLM}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_t} \left[ \frac{\alpha'_t}{1 - \alpha_t} \sum_{i:\, x_t^i = \mathtt{M}} -\log p_\theta(x_0^i \mid \mathbf{x}_t) \right].$$

That is: weighted BERT. The entire ELBO reduces to a schedule-aware mask-prediction loss, with the weight $\alpha'_t / (1 - \alpha_t)$ compensating for the fact that different diffusion times reveal different fractions of the sequence.

**Uniform-state.** Replace the absorbing token with a uniform distribution over $V$. A corrupted token is either itself or *a random other word*; there is no mask flag, so the denoiser never gets the comfort of knowing which positions are clean. The ELBO no longer collapses as neatly, and the Rao–Blackwellisation of MDLM fails. The *Diffusion Duality* paper (Sahoo et al., ICML 2025) rescued it by showing that uniform-state discrete diffusion is the pushforward of a Gaussian diffusion through a particular quantisation; their Theorem 3.1 gives a *tighter* ELBO than the Gaussian source, and the induced training objective is still tractable.

**Interpolating.** Eso-LM and its relatives mix the two: a fraction of tokens are masked, the rest uniformly corrupted. The design argument is that mask gives the denoiser a strong hint while uniform noise preserves contextual information. The 2026 scaling study says the design argument is wrong at scale.

## What the scaling study found

Fitting $\mathcal{L}(C) \approx a + b\, C^{-c}$ to loss as a function of training compute $C$, all four families — AR, masked (MDLM), uniform-state (Duo), interpolating (Eso-LM) — exhibit similar exponents $c$. What differs is the multiplicative offset. To match AR validation perplexity you spend, in terms of FLOPs, roughly $14\times$ with MDLM trained on the standard low-variance cross-entropy objective, $16\times$ with the true ELBO, $23\times$ with Duo, and $32\times$ with Eso-LM. These multipliers are stable across the sampled range from 100M to 1.7B.

The GSM8K result cuts the other way. Duo's validation perplexity is worse than MDLM's and much worse than AR's, but at 1.7B Duo posts the strongest GSM8K accuracy — above the AR baseline and above MDLM. Two observations are worth internalising. First, diffusion LMs can revise earlier tokens during sampling, and AR cannot. That is an architectural asymmetry that touches multi-step reasoning directly. Second, perplexity is informative *within* a diffusion family but misleading *across* families, because different corruption processes induce different effective loss functions on the same data. A cross-family perplexity comparison is comparing $\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)$ under different $q$.

## A concrete anchor

A one-step MDLM forward-and-loss, in a few readable lines, makes every term above tangible:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

V, L, B = 32_000, 512, 16
MASK = V  # mask-token id, outside the vocabulary

def forward_loss(x0, denoiser, eps=1e-3):
    t = torch.rand(x0.size(0), 1, device=x0.device).clamp(eps, 1 - eps)
    alpha = t                                   # linear schedule alpha_t = t
    keep = torch.bernoulli((1 - alpha).expand_as(x0.float())).bool()
    xt = torch.where(keep, x0, torch.full_like(x0, MASK))
    logits = denoiser(xt)                       # (B, L, V+1)
    logits[..., MASK] = -float("inf")           # SUBS: never predict MASK
    masked = (xt == MASK)
    weight = 1.0 / (1 - alpha)                  # alpha'_t = 1 under linear alpha
    nll = F.cross_entropy(
        logits.transpose(1, 2), x0, reduction="none"
    )                                           # (B, L)
    return (weight.squeeze(-1) * (nll * masked.float()).sum(-1)).mean()
```

The entire diffusion apparatus is a weighted masked-token cross-entropy with a mask-free output head. Every ablation in the scaling paper varies either the schedule $\alpha_t$, the parameterisation (carry-over on or off), the loss objective (true ELBO vs. the "simple" unweighted cross-entropy favoured in practice), or the forward kernel (absorbing vs. uniform vs. mixed). The expensive, architectural changes you might expect — new attention, new blocks — are almost never where the gains come from.

## What it implies in practice

Three habits to carry. First, a reported "diffusion LM beats AR on task $X$" with no matched-compute baseline is close to uninformative. The compute multiplier is dominated by constants, and the field now has them. Second, perplexity is a within-family metric. The right cross-family metric is downstream behaviour — reasoning accuracy, calibration, constrained-generation quality — and you should expect divergences from the perplexity ranking in exactly the cases that make a family interesting. Third, if your task has multi-step structure where revision helps (arithmetic, code, program synthesis, constrained decoding over a formal grammar), diffusion LMs are now worth benchmarking even when their validation loss looks worse than the AR competitor.

## Limits and open questions

Decoding compute dominates the honest comparison, and no one has cleanly isolated it. Diffusion LMs emit tokens in blocks and can run many denoising steps; AR LMs emit one token at a time with no revision. A compute-matched comparison that holds *training* compute fixed does not hold *inference* compute fixed. The newest inference-time methods for diffusion LMs — self-repulsive sampling (Helcig and Jaggi, September 2026) — report GSM8K plurality accuracy of 80.4% on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, up from 70.2% for the unpenalised decoder, at a cost that an AR model cannot pay in quite the same form. Whether the GSM8K wins in the scaling paper survive a *decoding*-compute match is open, and nothing yet rules out "diffusion LMs just use more inference FLOPs."

The parallel–sequential contradiction is sharper than the folk story. Chen et al. (October 2025, arXiv:2510.09544) argue that parallel scaling — sampling many trajectories at once — gives consistent gains for diffusion LMs on long chain-of-thought tasks, while sequential scaling (longer chains per trajectory) does *not*. The architecture that was supposed to make reasoning native may instead be particularly dependent on batch-time diversity. Under that reading, the GSM8K win at 1.7B is less about a reasoning-friendly inductive bias than about cheap parallelism in the denoising loop; the two are hard to tell apart without an ablation that holds trajectories fixed and varies decoding depth.

Finally, the compute multipliers are reported for a specific training recipe — cosine schedule, warmup, standard tokeniser, matched token budget. Other recipes narrow or widen the gap, and the 2026 paper does not claim universality. Treat $14\times$ as the current best-estimate constant, not a law. The scaling law is genuine; the leading constant is a measurement, and measurements update.

There is also a loss-function confound worth naming. The MDLM number quoted above refers to training with the simple, un-reweighted masked cross-entropy — not the true continuous-time ELBO. The ELBO is a few percent worse in compute terms, which is a small effect, but it points at a methodological choice the community has settled on quietly: the diffusion-LM literature now calls a particular low-variance surrogate "the diffusion loss," and the actual variational bound has become a baseline. A reader who knows only the surrogate may be surprised to find that the bound is looser; a reader who insists on the bound may find the surrogate better behaved. Either stance is defensible; conflating them is not.

## Further reading

- Subham Sekhar Sahoo et al., *Scaling Beyond Masked Diffusion Language Models*, arXiv:2602.15014, 2026 (ICML 2026). <https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15014>. The scaling-law paper. Read §4–5 for the compute-multiplier figures and §6 for GSM8K.
- Subham Sekhar Sahoo et al., *Simple and Effective Masked Diffusion Language Models*, NeurIPS 2024; arXiv:2406.07524. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07524>. MDLM. The SUBS derivation is in §3, and the reduction of the ELBO to a weighted BERT loss is the clearest exposition in the literature.
- Subham Sekhar Sahoo et al., *The Diffusion Duality*, ICML 2025; arXiv:2506.10892. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10892>. Shows uniform-state discrete diffusion as a quantised Gaussian and proves a tighter ELBO. Theorem 3.1 is the point.
- Aaron Lou, Chenlin Meng, and Stefano Ermon, *Discrete Diffusion Modeling by Estimating the Ratios of the Data Distribution*, ICML 2024; arXiv:2310.16834. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.16834>. SEDD. The alternative parameterisation that estimates concrete-score ratios rather than denoised categoricals; the reference when you care about the forward-kernel choice separately from the loss.
- Yair Schiff et al., *Simple Guidance Mechanisms for Discrete Diffusion Models*, arXiv:2412.10193, 2024. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.10193>. UDLM. The clean uniform-noise baseline that Duo generalises.
- Michael Helcig and Martin Jaggi, *Self-Repulsive Sampling for Diffusion Language Models*, arXiv:2609.39560, September 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39560>. The clearest inference-time method of 2026; its coverage/accuracy decomposition is the right template for thinking about diffusion-LM sampling budgets.
- Qiguang Chen et al., *Beyond Surface Reasoning: Unveiling the True Long Chain-of-Thought Capacity of Diffusion Large Language Models*, arXiv:2510.09544, October 2025. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09544>. Introduces the Parallel–Sequential Contradiction and separates parallel from sequential test-time scaling for diffusion LMs.
